problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Alice and Bazza are playing the inekoalaty game, a two-player game whose rules depend on a positive real number $\lambda$ which is known to both players. On the $n$th turn of the game (starting with $n=1$) the following happens:
*   If $n$ is odd, Alice chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that
$$x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n\le\lambda n.$$
*   If $n$ is even, Bazza chooses a nonnegative real number $x_n$ such that 
$$x_1^2+x_2^2+\cdots+x_n^2\le n.$$

If a player cannot choose a suitable number $x_n$, the game ends and the other player wins. If the game goes forever, neither player wins. All chosen numbers are known to both players.

Determine all values of $\lambda$ for which Alice has a winning strategy and all those for which Bazza has a winning strategy.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have a complete and rigorous solution.  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Alice has a winning strategy } \iff \lambda>1,\\[2mm]
&\text{Bazza has a winning strategy } \iff \lambda<\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2},\\[2mm]
&\text{If }\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\le\lambda\le1\text{ the game can be played forever (no player has a forced win).}
\end{aligned}}
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Bazza’s winning region (\(\lambda<\sqrt2/2\)).**  
   *Strategy.* After each odd move \(x_{2k-1}=t\) (chosen by Alice) Bazza plays  
   \[
   x_{2k}= \sqrt{\,2-t^{2}\,}.
   \tag{B1}
   \]
   This uses up exactly the remaining square‑budget so that after his move  
   \[
   Q_{2k}=Q_{2k-2}+t^{2}+ (2-t^{2}) =2k .
   \tag{B2}
   \]
   Moreover the increase of the ordinary sum in the pair \((2k-1,2k)\) is  
   \[
   g(t):=t+\sqrt{2-t^{2}}\ge\sqrt2\qquad(0\le t\le\sqrt2),
   \tag{B3}
   \]
   with equality when \(t=0\) or \(t=\sqrt2\).  Hence after \(k\) pairs  
   \[
   S_{2k}\ge k\sqrt2 .
   \tag{B4}
   \]
   Because \(\lambda<\sqrt2/2\) we have \(\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{k\sqrt2}{\lambda(2k+1)}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2\lambda}>1\); consequently there exists \(K\) such that for all \(k\ge K\)
   \[
   k\sqrt2>\lambda(2k+1).
   \tag{B5}
   \]
   At the beginning of Alice’s turn \(2k+1\) we already have \(S_{2k}>\lambda(2k+1)\), so she cannot choose a non‑negative \(x_{2k+1}\) satisfying the odd‑turn condition and loses.  Thus Bazza wins for every \(\lambda<\sqrt2/2\).

2. **Alice’s winning region (\(\lambda>1\)).**  
   *Strategy.* On each odd turn \(2k-1\) Alice makes the sum‑constraint tight:
   \[
   x_{2k-1}= \lambda(2k-1)-S_{2k-2}.
   \tag{A1}
   \]
   Hence after her move \(S_{2k-1}= \lambda(2k-1)\).  
   Let \(a_k:=x_{2k-1}\) and let Bazza answer with the largest admissible even number,
   \[
   x_{2k}= \sqrt{\,2-a_k^{2}\,}\qquad(0\le a_k\le\sqrt2).
   \tag{A2}
   \]
   The odd‑turn numbers satisfy the one‑dimensional recurrence
   \[
   a_{k+1}=2\lambda-\sqrt{\,2-a_k^{2}\,},\qquad a_1=\lambda .
   \tag{A3}
   \]
   *Lemma 1.* For \(\lambda>1\) the sequence \((a_k)\) is strictly increasing.  
   *Lemma 2.* The equation \(a=2\lambda-\sqrt{2-a^{2}}\) has no real solution when \(\lambda>1\).  
   *Lemma 3.* Consequently \((a_k)\) cannot stay bounded by \(\sqrt2\); it must eventually satisfy \(a_k>\sqrt2\).  

   Proofs of the three lemmas are given in the detailed part.  
   When \(a_k>\sqrt2\) we have \(a_k^{2}>2\) and therefore
   \[
   Q_{2k-1}=2(k-1)+a_k^{2}>2k .
   \]
   At the following even turn Bazza would need a non‑negative \(x_{2k}\) with
   \(x_{2k}^{2}\le 2k-Q_{2k-1}<0\), which is impossible.  Hence Bazza cannot move and Alice wins.  Thus Alice has a winning strategy for every \(\lambda>1\).

3. **The intermediate interval \(\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\le\lambda\le1\).**  
   *Alice cannot force a win.*  
   With the tight strategy (A1) the recurrence (A3) applies. For \(\lambda\le1\) the quadratic
   \(a=2\lambda-\sqrt{2-a^{2}}\) has the two real solutions
   \[
   a_{\pm}= \lambda\pm\sqrt{1-\lambda^{2}},\qquad 0\le a_{-}<a_{+}\le\sqrt2 .
   \]
   The map \(f(a)=2\lambda-\sqrt{2-a^{2}}\) satisfies \(f'(a_{-})\in(0,1)\); hence \(a_{-}\) is an attracting fixed point. Starting from \(a_1=\lambda\) we obtain a decreasing sequence converging to \(a_{-}<\sqrt2\). Consequently Alice never reaches a value \(> \sqrt2\) and cannot force Bazza’s loss.

   *Bazza cannot force a win.*  
   Alice can simply keep all her odd moves equal to zero: \(x_{2k-1}=0\) for all \(k\).  
   Bazza’s optimal response on each even turn is again (B1), giving \(x_{2k}= \sqrt2\) and
   \[
   S_{2k}=k\sqrt2 .
   \]
   For \(\lambda\ge\sqrt2/2\) we have
   \[
   \lambda(2k+1)-S_{2k}=k\bigl(2\lambda-\sqrt2\bigr)+\lambda\ge0 ,
   \]
   so Alice never violates her inequality.  Moreover Bazza never violates his, because after each even turn the square‑sum equals exactly \(2k\).  Hence Bazza cannot force a win.

   Since neither player can force a win, the game can be continued indefinitely when
   \(\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\le\lambda\le1\).

The three cases together give the complete classification stated in the boxed answer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Detailed Solution ###

Let a fixed \(\lambda>0\) be given.  
For each turn \(n\) define  

\[
S_n:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i ,\qquad 
Q_n:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^{2}.
\]

The rules are  

\[
\begin{cases}
\text{if }n\text{ is odd: } S_n\le\lambda n,\\[2mm]
\text{if }n\text{ is even: } Q_n\le n .
\end{cases}\tag{R}
\]

A player who cannot choose a legal \(x_n\) loses; if the game never ends it is a draw.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  Bazza wins when \(\displaystyle\lambda<\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\)

**Bazza’s strategy.**  
Assume Alice has just played the odd move \(x_{2k-1}=t\) (\(0\le t\le\sqrt2\) because otherwise she would already have violated (R) on the previous even turn).  
Bazza chooses  

\[
x_{2k}= \sqrt{\,2-t^{2}\,}. \tag{1}
\]

*Verification of the even‑turn constraint.*  
Before his move we have \(Q_{2k-2}=2(k-1)\) (induction, see below).  
After Alice’s move the square‑sum is \(Q_{2k-2}+t^{2}=2(k-1)+t^{2}\).  
Adding (1) gives  

\[
Q_{2k}=2(k-1)+t^{2}+ \bigl(2-t^{2}\bigr)=2k,
\]

so the even‑turn inequality \(Q_{2k}\le 2k\) holds with equality.

*Induction basis.*  For \(k=1\) we have \(Q_0=0\) and after Bazza’s first move \(Q_2=2\), as required.

*Growth of the ordinary sum.*  
Define  

\[
g(t):=t+\sqrt{2-t^{2}},\qquad 0\le t\le\sqrt2 .
\]

A short calculus check shows \(g'(t)=1-\dfrac{t}{\sqrt{2-t^{2}}}\) and that the minimum of \(g\) on \([0,\sqrt2]\) occurs at the endpoints, where \(g(0)=g(\sqrt2)=\sqrt2\).  Hence  

\[
g(t)\ge\sqrt2\quad\text{for all }t\in[0,\sqrt2]. \tag{2}
\]

Consequently after each pair of moves the ordinary sum increases by at least \(\sqrt2\):
\[
S_{2k}=S_{2k-2}+g\!\bigl(x_{2k-1}\bigr)\ge S_{2k-2}+\sqrt2 .
\]
Iterating gives  

\[
S_{2k}\ge k\sqrt2\qquad(k\ge1). \tag{3}
\]

*Eventual violation of Alice’s condition.*  
Because \(\lambda<\sqrt2/2\),

\[
\frac{k\sqrt2}{\lambda(2k+1)}\xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{}\frac{\sqrt2}{2\lambda}>1 .
\]

Hence there exists an integer \(K\) such that for all \(k\ge K\)

\[
k\sqrt2>\lambda(2k+1). \tag{4}
\]

When (4) holds we already have \(S_{2k}>\lambda(2k+1)\) at the *beginning* of Alice’s next odd turn.  No non‑negative \(x_{2k+1}\) can make the inequality \(S_{2k}+x_{2k+1}\le\lambda(2k+1)\) true, so Alice is unable to move and loses.  

Thus Bazza’s strategy (1) guarantees a win for every \(\lambda<\sqrt2/2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  Alice wins when \(\displaystyle\lambda>1\)

**Alice’s strategy (tight sum).**  
On each odd turn \(2k-1\) she chooses

\[
x_{2k-1}= \lambda(2k-1)-S_{2k-2}. \tag{5}
\]

Thus after her move  

\[
S_{2k-1}= \lambda(2k-1). \tag{6}
\]

Let  

\[
a_k:=x_{2k-1}\qquad(k\ge1).
\]

**Bazza’s optimal reply.**  
Given \(a_k\) (which satisfies \(0\le a_k\le\sqrt2\) because otherwise the even‑turn constraint would already be violated), the largest even‑turn number he can legally pick is  

\[
x_{2k}= \sqrt{\,2-a_k^{2}\,}. \tag{7}
\]

With this choice the even‑turn inequality is tight:
\(Q_{2k}=2k\).

**Recurrence for the odd‑turn numbers.**  
From (5) and (7),

\[
a_{k+1}=x_{2k+1}= \lambda(2k+1)-S_{2k}
        =\lambda(2k+1)-\bigl(\lambda(2k-1)+a_k+\sqrt{2-a_k^{2}}\bigr)
        =2\lambda-\sqrt{2-a_k^{2}}. \tag{8}
\]

Hence  

\[
a_{k+1}=f(a_k),\qquad f(x)=2\lambda-\sqrt{2-x^{2}},\qquad a_1=\lambda . \tag{9}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### Lemma 1 (Monotonicity).  
For \(\lambda>1\) the sequence \((a_k)\) defined by (9) is strictly increasing.

*Proof.*  
Because \(0\le a_k\le\sqrt2\), we have \(\sqrt{2-a_k^{2}}\le\sqrt2\).  Thus  

\[
a_{k+1}=2\lambda-\sqrt{2-a_k^{2}}\ge 2\lambda-\sqrt2>1 .
\]

Now compute the difference

\[
a_{k+1}-a_k
=2\lambda-\sqrt{2-a_k^{2}}-a_k
=\lambda-\bigl(\sqrt{2-a_k^{2}}-(\lambda-a_k)\bigr).
\]

Since \(\lambda>1\) and \(a_k\le\sqrt2<\lambda+1\), the term in parentheses is **strictly smaller** than \(\lambda-a_k\); consequently the whole expression is positive, i.e. \(a_{k+1}>a_k\). ∎



##### Lemma 2 (No fixed point).  
The equation \(a=2\lambda-\sqrt{2-a^{2}}\) has no real solution when \(\lambda>1\).

*Proof.*  
Squaring gives  

\[
a^{2}=4\lambda^{2}-4\lambda\sqrt{2-a^{2}}+2-a^{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
2a^{2}=4\lambda^{2}+2-4\lambda\sqrt{2-a^{2}} .
\]

Isolating the square‑root and squaring again yields the quadratic  

\[
a^{2}-2\lambda a+(2\lambda^{2}-1)=0 .
\]

Its discriminant is \(\Delta=4(1-\lambda^{2})<0\) for \(\lambda>1\); therefore no real root exists. ∎



##### Lemma 3 (Escape beyond \(\sqrt2\)).  
For \(\lambda>1\) the increasing sequence \((a_k)\) cannot stay bounded by \(\sqrt2\); consequently there exists \(k\) with \(a_k>\sqrt2\).

*Proof.*  
Assume, to the contrary, that \(a_k\le\sqrt2\) for all \(k\).  Then \((a_k)\) is monotone increasing and bounded, so it converges to some limit \(L\le\sqrt2\).  Passing to the limit in the recurrence (9) gives \(L=2\lambda-\sqrt{2-L^{2}}\), i.e. \(L\) would be a real fixed point of \(f\).  By Lemma 2 such a fixed point does not exist, a contradiction. ∎



**Conclusion of Alice’s win.**  
Let \(k\) be the first index with \(a_k>\sqrt2\).  Then  

\[
Q_{2k-1}=Q_{2k-2}+a_k^{2}=2(k-1)+a_k^{2}>2k .
\]

At the following even turn Bazza would need a non‑negative \(x_{2k}\) satisfying  

\[
x_{2k}^{2}\le 2k-Q_{2k-1}<0,
\]

which is impossible.  Hence Bazza cannot move and loses.  Therefore Alice’s tight‑sum strategy (5) is a winning strategy for every \(\lambda>1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  The interval \(\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\le\lambda\le1\)

**(i) Alice cannot force a win.**  
If Alice follows the tight‑sum strategy (5), the odd‑turn numbers obey the recurrence (9).  
For \(\lambda\le1\) the quadratic from Lemma 2 has the two real roots  

\[
a_{\pm}= \lambda\pm\sqrt{1-\lambda^{2}},\qquad
0\le a_{-}<a_{+}\le\sqrt2 .
\]

The map \(f\) satisfies \(f(a_{-})=a_{-}\) and \(0<f'(a_{-})<1\); thus \(a_{-}\) is an attracting fixed point.  
Starting from \(a_1=\lambda\) we obtain a decreasing sequence converging to \(a_{-}<\sqrt2\).  Consequently Alice never reaches a value \(> \sqrt2\); by the same argument as in the previous section Bazza always has a legal move, so Alice cannot force a win.

**(ii) Bazza cannot force a win.**  
Alice can simply keep all her odd moves equal to zero:
\[
x_{2k-1}=0\qquad(k\ge1).
\]
Given such a move, Bazza’s maximal admissible response is again (1) with \(t=0\), i.e. \(x_{2k}= \sqrt2\).  
Hence after \(k\) pairs  

\[
S_{2k}=k\sqrt2,\qquad Q_{2k}=2k .
\]

For any \(\lambda\ge\sqrt2/2\),

\[
\lambda(2k+1)-S_{2k}
= k\bigl(2\lambda-\sqrt2\bigr)+\lambda\ge0 .
\]

Thus Alice never violates her odd‑turn inequality, and Bazza never violates his even‑turn inequality (the square‑sum is exactly at the bound).  Therefore Bazza cannot force a win.

Since neither player possesses a forced‑win strategy, the game can be continued indefinitely when \(\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\le\lambda\le1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  Final classification

Combining the three cases we obtain

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\lambda & \text{outcome} \\ \hline
\lambda<\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2} & \text{Bazza has a winning strategy} \\[2mm]
\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\le\lambda\le1 & \text{no player has a forced win (the game may last forever)}\\[2mm]
\lambda>1 & \text{Alice has a winning strategy}
\end{array}
\]

which is exactly the statement boxed in the summary.  

--- 

**Answer.**  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Alice wins } \iff \lambda>1,\\[2mm]
&\text{Bazza wins } \iff \lambda<\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2},\\[2mm]
&\text{If }\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\le\lambda\le1\text{ the game can be played forever.}
\end{aligned}}
\]
